title: Perez Hilton and the end stage of the attention economy
snippet: The recent news surrounding Perez Hilton reveals an irony at the heart of the attention economy.
content_html:
The recent news surrounding Perez Hilton reveals an irony at the heart of the attention economy.

Hilton, the celebrity gossip columnist—famous for outing the sexuality of movie stars, and invading the private lives of public figures—was rushed to hospital after a severe mental health crisis, where he was found to be self-harming for fifteen minutes on a TikTok livestream.

Hilton rose to infamy at the dawn of Web 2.0—when the logic of the internet moved from one-sided communication, towards a participation-culture of user-based content. But his business model based on outrage and cruelty, once the preserve of a certain, particularly vindictive few—has been baked into the infrastructure of social media platforms. Now, when someone in the grips of a mental health crisis goes viral, and thousands of people in the comments start poking fun at them, you have to wonder, how did behaviour we once associated with the most malicious, tabloid-ish cobwebs of the internet, suddenly become an ordinary feature of online life?

Before attempting to answer that, it’s important to draw a distinction here. A lot of discourse around the Hilton situation frames what happened to him as poetic justice, or karma. For what it’s worth, I don’t align myself with that position. I don’t think any of us should be the arbiter of morality. We can say he never cared about anyone else in crisis, and while that’s true, if we offer no compassion when we see someone struggling, then we are no different than him, and we mirror the behaviour we turned into a bogeyman.

Attention is a limited resource, and we are living through a crisis of scarcity. Perez Hilton understood the economics of attention well. When we have more information at our disposal than ever, but our capacity to pay attention to it stays the same, it creates a deficit, which, in turn, creates competition. Hilton knew that humiliation, obscenity, sex scandals and nasty gossip were the easiest way to get us to look. It didn’t matter why we looked, so long as we paid attention. And this is the same logic we see in the algorithm on our social feeds. Like Hilton, the algorithm has no sense of morality, or personal integrity, only a shameless interest in what catches the eye. So if he can be cast as a sociopath, then so can the people who built these apps in his image.

The attention economy has consequences for what we get shown, and also, for how we look at it. When content reaches a saturation point, and we are bombarded by demands for our constant attention, we become desensitised to what we see on our screens. We can’t care about everything, so we detach as a way to protect ourselves. This detachment can sometimes look like dark humour or irony, and on its surface can seem callous and cruel, but when every doomscroll offers a fresh dystopia, irony becomes a filter to stop us from getting the tears in our eyes. But the insulation this irony affords us, also prevents us from seeing real suffering. When the context we find in the offline world collapses in a shareable Instagram reel, we are conditioned to consume everything with the same ironic distance. But I do think we’re de-programming ourselves as we become more media-literate, and we always have agency. On some level, we know that algorithms are designed to rage-bait us, divide us and keep us watching. And I think we are moving away from irony, because it gets stale after a while and it’s lazy. Irony is the centrist dad of personal emotions, because it is just a way to take a position without taking a position; to say something without admitting you mean it. I can feel us move towards hope again.

When I think of Hilton’s case, I think about the tyranny of the upload button. When social media platforms encouraged us to showcase every aspect of our personal lives, we didn’t have to read celebrity gossip columns anymore, we became gossip columnists of our own lives, with the ability to document our downfalls. When YouTube told us to “broadcast yourself” we were never told when the broadcast would end. So we publicised our private lives, until everything became see-through, our darkest traumas became storytime content, and we lived our life through the spectacle of a screen.

The attention economy is such an unforgiving machine, that by the time this article is published, nobody will be interested in reading about Perez Hilton anymore. In this environment, we are not allowed any time to reflect on ideas, or change our opinions—we need to report them live and direct, before we even get a chance to think. In this livestream-of-consciousness, everyone has to have a memorable hook, or a sticky buzzword, without leaving room for hesitation or nuance. But when the motivating factor of journalism becomes virality instead of conversation, we lose our creative integrity, and the common good gets clouded by click-through-rates.

In an ever-changing media landscape, immediacy is a poison that turns every tragedy into a momentary spectacle. Our life gets pulled into shareable fragments, 7 second clips because no one has time to listen to the full podcast anymore. So all surfaces are on display, illusions with nothing behind them, fighting for our attention in an overstimulated world.

At the end stage of the attention economy, we see everything, but take none of it in. Whether it’s Perez Hilton, or your Instagram feed, we remain spectators, and in this immersive theatre, the coliseum might have collapsed, but the broadcast never ends.
